The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
By the 650s, the conquests had reached parts of North Africa and the island of Cyprus.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This marked the end of the first of the two main stages of Arab expansion.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The second stage stretched from the late seventh century into the early eighth century.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
By then, the Arab state had gained control over vast territories in Asia, Africa, and Europe, after a movement of conquest that had continued for more than seventy years.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

At this point, we should look at some of the explanations given by European scholars in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries for the Arab-Islamic conquests and for the remarkable victories they achieved.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
One explanation claimed that Islamic religious fanaticism drove the Arabs of the peninsula to wage wars against non-Muslim countries.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Another said that Arabia contained too many people and too little food, so conquest was a way of solving this imbalance.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

In the twentieth century, some Orientalists argued that drought had left the Arabian desert short of water and grazing land. The people therefore lacked enough food, and their animals lacked enough pasture. According to this view, they left Arabia in search of a better life in more fertile countries.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The explanation based on religious fanaticism can be rejected for a simple reason.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

For large numbers of the soldiers in the Arab-Islamic armies, Islam had not yet taken such deep root in their minds that they would willingly risk their lives for the sole purpose of forcing the Islamic faith on the people of the countries they conquered and abolishing the religions those people already followed.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
If that had really been the purpose, the conquerors would have accepted nothing from the defeated populations except conversion to Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the historical record clearly shows otherwise.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Arab conquerors allowed the people of the conquered lands to keep their religions and beliefs in return for paying the jizya tax.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They were also allowed to continue practicing their religious rituals.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Indeed, religious freedom was included among the protections granted to them, and Christian clergy in particular were often treated well.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The reality is that tribal loyalties were still more deeply rooted than Islamic ideas, beliefs, and principles among many of the soldiers taking part in the conquests.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Many of them also knew very little about those ideas and principles.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
How, then, can anyone reasonably explain the wars of conquest mainly through religious fanaticism while ignoring the material conditions behind them?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Two of those material conditions were already recognized in the explanations mentioned above: the imbalance between a growing population and limited food supplies, and the harsh climate of Arabia, which encouraged people to seek better living conditions in fertile lands beyond the peninsula.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But there was another historical factor that made these pressures much more powerful.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Trade inside Arabia had been developing.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Between the sixth and seventh centuries CE, a class of wealthy Arab merchants had begun to grow rapidly.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Their rise contained the beginnings of a new society built around commercial social relations.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This group was the earliest class form of that new society.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
By the time Islam appeared, the group was growing so quickly that the internal limits of the Arabian Peninsula were becoming too narrow for its development.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Expansion beyond Arabia was therefore becoming a necessity.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Islam, as a universal movement, helped awaken and strengthen these ambitions for expansion.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In this sense, it appeared as an objective response to that historical need.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We now face a major question.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
How were the Arabs able to win such great victories against the huge regular armies of the two most powerful and highly developed states of the seventh century, Persia and Byzantium?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Arabs were leaving their peninsula for the first time as conquering soldiers.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Their own society had also not reached the same level of development as some of the peoples whose lands they were now conquering and bringing under Arab-Islamic rule.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This question was asked long ago.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
And the answer has also existed for a long time in the form of historical facts that point directly toward the real explanation.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

These facts give us an almost complete picture of the economic, social, and political conditions facing the two great empires on one side, and the peoples confronted by the Arab conquerors on the other.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They also help us separate two sides of the explanation.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
First, there were objective conditions—conditions independent of what the Arabs themselves wanted or intended.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Second, there were subjective factors on the Arab side: the qualities and motivations that allowed them to take advantage of those conditions.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
What were these objective historical conditions?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
And what were the subjective strengths of the Arabs?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Let us begin with the first question.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
When the Arab-Islamic conquests began, Byzantium and Persia had already been badly weakened by long wars against one another in regions lying around or near the Arabian Peninsula.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
These regions included Mesopotamia, or Iraq, and Persia on one side, and Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Turkey, and North Africa, which were then under Byzantine control, on the other.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The long wars had weakened both empires.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In addition, the Byzantine state and the church connected with it were carrying out a form of religious persecution in Egypt, Syria, and Palestine.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At the time, the Byzantine emperor Heraclius was in Syria and was imposing extremely heavy taxes on the population.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Bitterness against these conditions had spread widely, and people could see no clear way out.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Feudal exploitation of those who produced society’s wealth became mixed with religious persecution.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Syrian clergy faced pressure from the Byzantine Church, which had made Syria one of its major centers.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This produced opposition among Syrian churchmen to foreign Byzantine rule.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Different local Christian sects and communities gathered around this opposition.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The movement therefore had a social content expressed through a religious form.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Peasants and craftsmen were drawn to it, and it gradually took on a class character as well.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Economic, social, political, and religious conditions like these made war much harder for a regular imperial army.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
That army now had to face an advancing force of irregular conquerors without being able to rely on support from the local population.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It was surrounded by a hostile population.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This created conditions for an internal psychological war among its own soldiers against the state whose oppressive rule they were being asked to defend.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We can therefore make three comparisons.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
First, compare the morale of an attacking army with the morale of an army forced onto the defensive.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Second, compare forces carrying the energy of something new and growing with forces carrying the decline of something old and dying.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Third, compare fighters driven by powerful hopes of reaching a richer life with soldiers who have been forced into service while suppressing their own resentment against the state they are defending.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Ibn Khaldūn tried to explain why Muslim armies, despite their small numbers and limited equipment, defeated “the armies of Persia at al-Qādisiyya and the armies of Heraclius at al-Yarmūk,” even though those opposing forces were incomparably larger and better equipped.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In substance, his explanation is not very far from the three comparisons we have just made, even though the historical form in which he understood the issue was naturally different.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Because they lived nearby, the people of Syria and Mesopotamia must have heard something about Islam’s call to reduce the material suffering of the poor, the destitute, and the oppressed.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The peoples of these regions must also have hoped for some movement that could free them from the unbearable conditions under which they were living.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This became visible during the Arab conquest of Syria.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Popular resentment there had already developed into political and social opposition to Byzantine rule.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
That opposition had a clearly religious form.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Local Christian sects had emerged among the native population and united in opposition to the Byzantine Church, which expressed the ideology of the occupying political power in religious language.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Peasants and craftsmen supported these religious groups because of their own anger toward Byzantine rule.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Through that opposition, they also resisted, in a largely spontaneous way, the feudal ideology represented religiously by the Byzantine Church.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
One fact makes this especially clear.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Under Byzantine rule in Syria, Palestine, and Egypt, local Christian clergy were prevented from holding the highest church offices.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Those positions were reserved for Greek clergy.

4 — Arab-Islamic Rule in the Conquered Lands
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We must also remember that when the Arabs left the peninsula as conquerors, their own society had not yet fully developed into the kind of class society that already existed in the conquered lands.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In those countries, production was already organized mainly through feudal relations of an eastern type.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This created a wide gap between the economic and social structure of the conquered societies and the political and administrative system of their new Arab rulers.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Arab conquerors had never before governed societies with this kind of social and economic structure.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In other words, early Islamic Arab rule did not naturally arise from the economic and social conditions already present in those countries.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
How, then, did the Arab conquerors actually govern the peoples they had defeated?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
During the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and especially under ʿUmar, their policy took the following form.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
First, the conquerors took the booty captured from defeated enemy armies on the battlefield.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Under Islamic rules of war, this booty was divided between the fighters and the Bayt al-Māl, the public treasury.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Four-fifths went to the fighters, while the remaining fifth went to the treasury.
